description: Amamos tecnologia e tudo o que ela nos permite criar. Gostamos de transformar ideias em soluções inteligentes, desenvolver projetos, experimentar novas possibilidades e encontrar maneiras de tornar as coisas mais simples, eficientes e inovadoras. Para nós, tecnologia não é apenas código ou máquinas, é criatividade, conhecimento e a vontade de construir algo que realmente faça a diferença.
summary:
PULSAR is a web app that lets astronauts monitor their own health and act on it, even when Earth is too far away to help in time. It organizes health around NASA’s five hazards of human spaceflight: space radiation, isolation and confinement, distance from Earth, altered gravity, and hostile closed environments.

Each crew member does a 30-second daily check-in (sleep, mood, stress, vital signs, exercise, symptoms) and a reaction test that measures fatigue. Instead of comparing results to Earth reference ranges, PULSAR compares each astronaut to their own baseline and flags deviations and worsening trends. Every alert becomes a clear action card telling the crew what to do now.

Reports to the flight surgeon travel with the real communication delay of the mission, so the crew learns to decide autonomously. On a Mars mission, a reply can take over 20 minutes: early, on-board detection is what keeps a small problem from becoming an emergency.
details:
PULSAR is a responsive web app that runs on the spacecraft’s own server, so it keeps working with no link to Earth. It is built around NASA’s five hazards of human spaceflight, and the dashboard shows one status per hazard (Normal, Caution, Alert).

  • Daily check-in (30 seconds): sleep, mood, stress, heart rate, blood pressure, oxygen saturation, temperature, body mass, exercise and symptoms.
  • Reaction test: a 1 or 3 minute vigilance test, done by tapping the screen, that measures fatigue.
  • Personal baseline: each astronaut is compared to their own first entries, not to Earth reference ranges. The app flags values that deviate from that baseline and trends that worsen over four entries in a row.
  • Action cards: every alert explains what to do now and links to the related NASA or CSA resource.
  • Ground reports with delay: a report to the flight surgeon and the reply both travel with the mission’s communication delay (about 1 second in low Earth orbit, 12 minutes one way to Mars).
  • Mission scenarios: low Earth orbit, lunar surface or Mars transit, each with its own radiation dose rate and delay, plus simulated events (solar particle event, CO2 removal failure).
  • Three roles: crew member, crew medical officer (sees the whole crew, sorted by who needs attention) and flight surgeon on the ground.

Benefits

The crew sees problems early, in plain language, and knows the next step without waiting for Earth. The medical officer gets a single view of the crew. The ground team receives a short summary instead of raw data, and detailed records stay on board, which protects the astronaut’s privacy.

Intended impact

On missions to the Moon and Mars, real-time medical support is not possible. PULSAR aims to move health monitoring from “ground watches the crew” to “the crew watches itself”, so a small change in sleep, heart rate or attention is handled before it becomes an emergency. The same approach can serve remote places on Earth, such as research stations, ships and isolated communities.

Tools and technologies

PHP 8 with PDO, SQLite (MySQL also supported), HTML, CSS and vanilla JavaScript. Charts and icons are hand-written SVG, with no external libraries or CDNs, so the app works fully offline. It is installable as a Progressive Web App, available in English, Portuguese and Spanish, with dark and light themes. No dedicated hardware is required: any phone, tablet or laptop with a browser.

Creative aspect

  • Health is judged against the astronaut’s own normal, because the body changes in space and Earth ranges can mislead.
  • Communication delay is something the user experiences: the reply really does take time to arrive, and the crew cannot see that it is on its way.
  • A fatigue test that needs no sensor, only a tap.
  • The five hazards work as the navigation of the app, so NASA’s own framework becomes the interface.

Factors we considered

  • Autonomy: everything must work without Earth.
  • Crew time: the check-in takes 30 seconds, and blank fields are allowed.
  • Clarity: status is shown by colour, shape and text, never colour alone.
  • Privacy: each crew member sees only their own data, and chooses what is sent to the ground.
  • Accessibility and reach: three languages, two themes, and a layout that works on a phone.
  • Honesty about data: the crew, their health records and the cabin sensors in this version are simulated. Radiation rates, CO2 limits and thresholds are approximate reference values that need validation against NASA standards before any real use.

Use of AI: the code, interface texts, translations and video were developed with the assistance of Claude (Anthropic). The video narration is AI-generated speech (Piper TTS). No NASA branding is used.
